explanation: This patient has a slowly progressive seventh cranial nerve (CN VII) palsy, which is highly suggestive of a neoplastic etiology. Neoplasms may involve the seventh nerve in the cerebellopontine angle (eg, acoustic neuroma, meningioma), within the fallopian canal, or in the parotid gland. Bell palsy represents the most common type of facial neuropathy, but presents with sudden onset of facial paresis and not a gradual onset. Herpes zoster involving the seventh nerve is called Ramsay Hunt syndrome and also presents with an acute onset of facial paralysis. Sarcoidosis can aﬀect the seventh nerve, but often responds to steroids.

explanation: Pituitary apoplexy results from hemorrhage or infarction in a pituitary adenoma; it can occur spontaneously or after head trauma. question: A 25-year-old woman with headache and blurred vision underwent a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan that demonstrated a pineal tumor (Figure 1). She has 20/20 acuity OU and 5 mm pupils OU with minimal reaction to light stimulus (direct and consensual). What additional pupillary ﬁnding may be detected with further testing?

options.A: segmental (nasal) pupil constriction with slit-lamp exam
options.B: pupil constriction in a dark room (paradoxical pupils)

explanation: The pineal gland is located dorsal and rostral to the pretectal nuclei and posterior commissure of the midbrain, where parasympathetic ﬁbers mediating pupillary constriction to light are found (Figure 2). When compression from pineal gland tumors damages the dorsal midbrain, the parasympathetic light reﬂex pathway is disrupted, and the pupil does not constrict to light. In contrast, the ﬁbers in the near reﬂex pathway approach the pretectal nucleus from the ventral aspect of the midbrain. Thus, dorsal midbrain damage can result in midsize pupils with poor light response and preserved near response. Associated ﬁndings include bilateral eyelid retraction (Collier sign), vertical gaze palsy, accommodative paresis, and convergence-retraction nystagmus (Parinaud syndrome). Pupil constriction in a dark room (paradoxical pupils) is a clinical sign of congenital and/or inherited retinal dystrophies (eg, congenital stationary night blindness). Poor pupillary constriction to 1% pilocarpine in a patient with ﬁxed and dilated pupils suggests pharmacologic mydriasis. Segmental pupil constriction with slit-lamp examination suggests segmental iris sphincter paralysis, a feature of Adie tonic pupil.

explanation: Altitudinal visual ﬁeld defect is the most common visual ﬁeld defect seen in NAION. question: A patient is asked to ﬁxate in downgaze for a few seconds and then look straight ahead. When this happens, there is an upward overshoot of the eyelid before the eyelid settles back to the baseline position. What is this sign called?

explanation: This child's clinical features are characteristic of Horner syndrome. explanation: CT is superior to MRI in detecting bony deformities, especially in the orbits and sinuses. Therefore, orbital fractures are best seen on orbital CT rather than on MRI, as CT allows detailed views of fracture location in relation to soft tissue. "Chiasmal lesion" is not correct, because axial CT often misses pituitary abnormalities. question: A 12-year-old boy presents with sudden vision loss in the right eye. His visual acuity was no light perception (NLP) in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. There was no relative aﬀerent pupillary defect (RAPD); nonorganic vision loss is suspected. What test performed in clinic may help demonstrate normal 20/20 vision in the right eye in this patient?
explanation: Although all of the listed techniques may help uncover functional visual loss in a patient claiming monocular NLP vision, only the fogging test can demonstrate 20/20 vision in the eye with suspected nonorganic vision loss. To perform the fogging test, the clinician employs a trial frame with plus and minus cylinder (6 diopters), which have their axes aligned; these are placed in front of the patient's "good" eye. The patient is then asked to read the Snellen chart while one of the cylinder lenses is rotated. The cylinder rotation will severely blur vision as the 2 axes are rotated out of alignment. If the patient continues to read the 20/20 line, he or she is doing so with the "bad" eye. The fogging test is a form of confusion testing, which requires the patient to be unaware of which eye is actually tested. Other confusion tests including the duochrome test (in which the patient wears duochrome/Worth 4-dot glasses and attempts to read letters through the red/green ﬁlter on the Snellen chart; if all the letters are read, then vision is normal in both eyes) and the polarized lens test (in which the examiner uses the Snellen chart projected through polarized ﬁlters; if all the letters are read, then vision is normal in both eyes). The mirror test can demonstrate at least light perception vision, but it would not help prove he has 20/20 vision. Movement on optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) drum indicates 20/400 vision, but it cannot determine if the vision is any better than 20/400. A base-out prism test showing movement when the prism is placed over the "bad" eye indicates some vision in that eye, but it cannot prove 20/20 vision.

question: A 44-year-old woman with a history of diabetes develops a third nerve palsy, which is diagnosed as microvascular by her local physician. options.C: immediate neuroimaging to rule out a compressive lesion

explanation: Lid elevation on attempted downgaze indicates aberrant regeneration of the third cranial nerve, which occurs as damaged axons regrow to innervate muscles other than those they originally innervated. This ﬁber misrouting produces synkinetic phenomena, including eyelid retraction with adduction or pupillary miosis with elevation, adduction, or depression. Aberrant regeneration may result after trauma or from compression of the nerve from tumor or aneurysm. Aberrant regeneration does not occur with microvascular ischemia. Even in a diabetic patient in whom third nerve palsy is initially consistent with ischemic vasculopathy, development of this ﬁnding should prompt urgent neuroimaging to rule out a compressive etiology that requires treatment. Continued follow-up for 6 months to check for resolution would be appropriate in a complete non-pupil-involving third nerve palsy in a vasculopathic patient with no signs of aberrancy. While more aggressive treatment of diabetes may be appropriate in these patients, it will not address the immediate concern of a more dire cause of the palsy. question: What clinical ﬁnding is consistent with aberrant regeneration of CN III? lateral region of the brainstem disrupts the sensory pathways; therefore, Wallenberg syndrome is a type of stroke without paralysis. Patients can present with these signs and symptoms: ipsilateral loss of facial pain and temperature sensation (involvement of the descending tract of CN V) contralateral loss of hemibody pain and temperature sensation (involvement of the lateral spinothalamic tract) ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia (damage to spinocerebellar tracts) ipsilateral ﬁrst-order Horner syndrome ipsilateral ocular tilt reaction (head tilt toward the side of the lesion) In addition, patients can have dysarthria, dysphagia, vertigo, or persistent hiccups; there is no extremity weakness. Although the lateral medulla is in the distribution of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), Wallenberg syndrome usually results from occlusion of the more proximal vertebral artery. Consequently, patients may experience lateropulsion, the sensation of being pulled toward the side of the lesion, which results from damage to the CN VIII nuclei. Patients may also manifest ocular lateropulsion; this eﬀect can be tested by examination of horizontal pursuit and saccadic movements, which will reveal a bias that produces hypermetric movements toward the side of the lesion and hypometric movements away from the side of the lesion. Vertical saccades may follow an elliptical path as the eyes deviate toward the side of the lesion during the vertical movement. Finally, this directional bias also can be observed by noting that the eyes turn toward the side of the lesion after visual ﬁxation is removed for a few seconds.
explanation: Aberrant regeneration of CN III occurs after damage results in regrowth and misrouting of ﬁbers with innervation of muscles not normally activated together. This causes abnormal synkinetic phenomenon such as eyelid retraction with adduction or pupillary miosis with supraduction, adduction, or infraduction. Eyelid retraction with supraduction is a normal response to CN III activation. Aberrant regeneration of CN III is common after traumatic injury, but can also occur with compressive lesions such as aneurysms and tumors. Microvascular ischemic CN III does not cause aberrant regeneration.

question: What pupillary abnormality may be present in an optic tract lesion?

Pupillomotor ﬁbers travel in the optic tract and exit just before the lateral geniculate nucleus for the brachium of the superior colliculus. When an optic tract lesion occurs, it can damage both pupillomotor and visual ﬁbers, resulting in a contralateral visual ﬁeld defect and relative aﬀerent pupillary defect. Light-near dissociation can occur with dorsal midbrain lesions. Sympathetic nerves do not travel in the optic tract, and a tract lesion does not cause a Horner syndrome. question: What feature characterizes the mydriasis caused by Adie pupil?

question: In the condition known as crocodile tears, through which nerve are ﬁbers originally supplying the mandibular and sublingual glands redirected to the lacrimal gland?
explanation: After any facial neuropathy, but most commonly as a result of Bell palsy, regenerating axons may reinnervate diﬀerent muscles from those originally served; such aberrant regeneration can cause synkinetic movements. Disorders of aberrant facial innervation include lacrimation caused by chewing (crocodile tears), in which ﬁbers originally supplying mandibular and sublingual glands reinnervate the lacrimal gland by way of the greater superﬁcial petrosal nerve. This syndrome usually develops after severe injury to the proximal CN VII and may be accompanied by decreased reﬂex tearing and decreased ability to taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. In another example, when axons originally destined for the orbicularis oculi reinnervate the lower facial muscles, each blink may cause a twitch of the corner of the mouth or a dimpling of the chin. Conversely, movements of the lower face—such as pursing the lips, smiling, or chewing with the mouth closed—may produce involuntary eyelid closure. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) accounts for nearly 50% of cases with intracranial hemorrhage. Its incidence increases with age, and it is more common in women. African American and Hispanic individuals have a higher incidence of SAH when compared with white individuals. Most SAHs result from saccular, or "berry," aneurysms. Only a minority of cases of SAH are nonaneurysmal in etiology. Approximately 85% of congenital saccular, or "berry," aneurysms develop in the anterior part of the circle of Willis. The origin of the posterior communicating artery from the internal carotid artery is the most common site. Such an aneurysm typically presents with headache and third cranial nerve palsy involving the pupil. Vascular malformations within and on the surface of the brain parenchyma constitute approximately 7% of cases of subarachnoid hemorrhage and arise from capillary telangiectasias, cavernous hemangiomas, venous angiomas, or AVMs. SAH usually presents with abrupt onset severe headache that is typically described by patients as the "worst headache of my life." The headache occurs in 97% of cases; 30% have symptoms lateralized to the side of the hemorrhage. The combination of vitreous hemorrhage and subarachnoid hemorrhage (Terson syndrome) portends a worse prognosis. Maintaining a high index of suspicion and evaluating the patient with noncontrast CT, followed by mandatory lumbar puncture if CT results are negative, are essential in making the diagnosis. Digital subtraction angiography is superior to CT or MRA for the detection of SAH due to aneurysm. Terson syndrome is a vitreous and sub-ILM or subhyaloid hemorrhage caused by an abrupt intracranial hemorrhage. Although the exact mechanism is not known, it is suspected that the acute intracranial hemorrhage causes an acute rise in the intraocular venous pressure, resulting in a rupture of peripapillary and retinal vessels. Approximately one-third of patients with subarachnoid or subdural hemorrhage have associated intraocular hemorrhage, which may include intraretinal and subretinal bleeding. Terson syndrome occurs primarily in individuals between 30 and 50 years old, but it can occur at any age. In most cases, the visual function is unaﬀected once the hemorrhage clears. Spontaneous improvement generally occurs, although vitrectomy is occasionally required to clear the ocular media. Pupillary dysfunction with CN III palsy results from loss of parasympathetic input and produces a mid-dilated pupil that responds poorly to light. Patients may present with variable dysfunction of the levator palpebrae or extraocular muscles. Aneurysms that arise at the junction of the posterior communicating artery (PCoA) and internal carotid artery (ICA) are juxtaposed to CN III and are, therefore, in a position to produce a CN III palsy as the initial manifestation of aneurysmal expansion or rupture. Pupillary involvement occurs because the pupillomotor ﬁbers reside superﬁcially in the medial aspect of the nerve adjacent to the PCoA. Thus, until proven otherwise, the clinician must assume that a nontraumatic CN III palsy with pupillary involvement or evidence of progression to pupillary involvement is secondary to an aneurysm. Although B-scan ultrasonography may be useful to evaluate the posterior pole, neuroimaging is the most important imaging study for the initial consideration. explanation: Infantile nystagmus syndrome (INS), also called congenital nystagmus, is classically described as a binocular conjugate horizontal nystagmus that presents within the ﬁrst 2 years of life. Congenital motor nystagmus (CMN) is not associated with aﬀerent pathway disease, is often associated with normal or near-normal vision, has a normal ocular examination and normal neuroimaging, and does not produce oscillopsia. In contrast, sensory nystagmus arises when central visual acuity is too poor to develop a stable ﬁxational mechanism. Sensory nystagmus is associated with conditions that cause bilateral, pregeniculate vision loss in children younger than 2 years. Approximately two-thirds of CMN patients exhibit a paradoxical inversion of the optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) response, which is unique to CMN. Normally, when a patient with right-jerk nystagmus views an optokinetic drum rotation to the patient's left (eliciting a "pursuit left, jerk right" response), the intensity of the right-jerk nystagmus increases.
